explanation: No single theme. It fires strongly on HTTP header names (Authorization, Cookie, HttpMethod), config keys ('step'), biomedical word pieces (macro-ph-ages, endosc-op-ic, Squ-amous, reverse phase), and assorted English function words ('according to', 'brought to', 'child with'). Mid and weak activations are scattered.

Fires on tokens inside hexadecimal hash or ID strings (git hashes, GUIDs, Unity guid fields, sha256 oids, memory addresses, hex segments in URLs), usually on a hex digit or letter a few characters into the string. Ordinary text does not activate it, and plain numbers only barely.

Fires on a noun naming someone's place, role or occupation that follows a possessive or a motion verb, most strongly 'home' (her home, returning home, call home, home planet/turf), and also 'work', 'duty', 'job', 'life' and 'what he does'. Possessive pronouns on their own give weak activation.

Mostly fires on prepositions and relative words ('in', 'on', 'to', 'that', 'as', 'into') right after a noun phrase in technical or Q&A prose, as in 'a file in', 'the LICENSE file that', 'used to'. It also fires on odd subword pieces in names and code (Plesk, fast, i2s, onAfterFind). The pattern is diffuse.

Fires in software copyright and license headers on the end of the copyright-holder line, chiefly the period after the company or author name ('Microsoft Corporation.', 'Authors.') and the word 'reserved' or 'Reserved' in 'All rights reserved'. Weaker on other code-boundary tokens such as closing tags or brackets.

Fires on 'See' (or 'see', 'refer to') that starts a cross-reference sentence in license boilerplate: 'See the License for...', 'See LICENSE.txt', 'see the file COPYING'. More weakly it fires on similar pointers in prose ('Check out', 'Click', 'please view', 'read our guide').

Fires on a word piece or word in the middle of a multi-token term or name, often a technical or biomedical term (neuro-logic, phosph-ol-ipids, scala tym-pani, RT-PCR, PTP) or a proper name (Tokyo, Hanoi, Parity). It seems to respond to the continuation of a specialized term rather than to any meaning. Fairly diffuse.

Fires on titles and honorifics that come right before a person's name, especially the period of abbreviated titles ('Gov.', 'Rep.', 'Rev.') and words like Judge, Cardinal, Rabbi, Archdeacon, Datuk and colonel. It is weaker on job titles in apposition (CEO, Secretary, director, chairman) and on bare role nouns.

Fires on a word inside a noun phrase that points to a specific, still-unknown item, such as 'the precise/exact/underlying/optimal ...', 'the patient group that', and indirect-question words ('when', 'who', 'how', 'what'). It also fires on the key name in config or identifier strings and on 'license' in 'copyright and license information'. The core is somewhat loose.

Mixed. It fires on capital-letter or subword pieces of names and codes (Z in Zune, Zych and Zelenskiy, IL in gene names, -ov-, Max in minMaxIdx, 8 in ISO-8859, 9 in Itanium 9700) and on certain connectives in technical prose ('recognize and', 'include', 'code division', Spanish 'antes de'). No clear common feature.

Mostly fires on the preposition after a methods-style participle in scientific prose: 'as assessed/measured by', 'controlling for', 'detected using', 'count as'. It also fires on assorted mid-compound pieces (miniatur-ization, Typed-Array, Reactive Oxygen, polyc-yst-ic). The main job is clear, but there are unrelated extras.

Fires on the bare infinitive 'be' after a modal verb or 'to' ('can be', 'will be', 'should be', 'going to be', 'need to be'). It is moderate on 'been' after 'have' or 'has' and weak on 'to' after verbs like 'expected'.

Mixed. It fires on whitespace or indentation tokens and line breaks in code, pieces of code identifiers, LaTeX tokens, and word starts in prose (Things, Environmental, Cal, calque). No unifying feature is visible.

Fires on function words and nouns in casual or discussion text ('lots of', 'grateful for the', 'wrong questions', 'much to talk about', 'chances are you'). Nothing clearly distinguishes these contexts.

Mainly fires on 'or' (also 'and' or a comma) joining two alternatives in a coordination, especially between numbers ('5 or 6', '3 or 4', '50 years or longer', 'Qt 5.1 or higher'). It also fires on the noun repeated in such pairs ('individual or agency', 'equipment or machine') and on list items in arrays.

Fires on 'following' (also 'below') when it points forward to content that comes next ('the following disclaimer', 'the following lines', 'listed in the following'). It also fires on the first content word of a doc-comment or heading ('Helper functions', 'Utility class', 'Component List').

Fires on the main verb or auxiliary ('is', 'has', 'have', 'are') right after the subject of the first sentence of an article or description, especially when the subject is a named entity or product introduced at the start of a document (Kuala Lumpur has, Hackett is). Weaker for subject-verb positions later in the text.

Fires on middle subword pieces of proper names and uncommon or foreign words that are split into several tokens (Green-bl-att, Al-bre-cht, Lux-emb-urg, Klob-uchar), including German, Danish and Portuguese words. Common English words do not activate it.

Fires on inner word pieces of biochemical or biological technical terms (ty-ros-ine, perox-is-ome, flag-ell-um, car-box-ylase, glucopyran-os-ide), usually on a Latin or Greek root fragment. It is weak on other jargon and on names.

Fires on tokens in programming Q&A and code, especially pieces of software or tool names (XAMPP, Aptana, wamp, TortoiseSVN, JENKINS) and indentation or code keywords. The pattern is loosely 'inside technical identifiers in developer text', with no sharper common feature.
